## Starts with an Overview of HCI

## Through what lens do you view HCI?
- Historical
- Disciplines
- Communities
- Technical
- Methods
- Industrial
- Economic

## Historical
- Antecedents emerged in WWII aircraft design
- HCI itself emerged in the 1980s
- Mostly founded by cognitive psychologists
- Science was defunded by the Reagan administration
- Military still had funding
- Cognitive psychologists were hired by the military to explore phenomena like *flaming* in email

## Disciplines
- HCI is a multidisciplinary field
- Engineers, Computer scientists, psychologists, sociologists, anthropologists, designers all came together, especially around the CHI conference

## Communities
- HCI is a community
- Human factors in engineering schools is a related community
- MIS scholars in business schools is a related community

## Technical
- HCI's early practitioners were keenly interested in expensive hardware and how to make the most of it
- Later practitioners took advantage of plummeting hardware costs to develop hardware / software solutions to more marginal problems

## Methods
- HCI has a rich history of methods
- The book *Ways of Knowing in HCI* covers over a dozen methods used by HCI researchers to understand human-computer interaction

## Industrial
- HCI has been practiced in industry almost as long as in academia
- Apple was an early hotbed of HCI research in the 1980s
- Today, it seems that more HCI PhDs work in industry than in academia

## Economic
- In some ways, the story of HCI has been the story of plummeting hardware costs:
- Early researchers were concerned with a single user, making the most of expensive hardware, measuing tasks minutely
- As costs plummeted, researcher became interested in discretionary computer use
- Eventually, workgroups became a focus as cheap networks proliferated
- Later, communities of practice (joined by interest but geographically dispersed) and communities of life (geographically concentrated) became a focus
- Today, many HCI researchers are focused on society in general as computing permeates every aspect of our lives

# Why HCI?

## Why should we care about HCI?
- It's difficult to design good systems
- Partly because of the multidisciplinary nature of systems
- Partly because it's hard to understand human behavior
- Partly because technology changes so rapidly
- People were awakened to these reasons in the mid 1980s by the publication of *The Psychology of Everyday Things*, soon renamed *Design of Everyday Things*

## Who cares about HCI?
- Today I was talking to someone who does HCI at Geico
- You might be surprised by the number of companies that have *design systems*, an artifact of HCI practice
- Every major school of computing has at least one HCI researcher, while some, like CMU, UW, UMich, Georgia Tech, and our own school, have many
- Most governments have HCI researchers and practitioners, as do many non-profits
- They are often brought together by organizations like NIST and ISO to establish standards

# Isn't technology changing too fast to study?
- Technology changes, but human behavior doesn't change as fast
- HCI researchers and practitioners have found that there are enduring principles
- Some of the ideas you will study in this course come from the 1950s, like Fitts's Law, but still matter now and in the future
- We'll try to focus on the enduring principles, although we may often sample the *flavor of the month*
